Definitive 5,000-word guide to visual testing and RVI for welds, vessels, pipework and turbines. Covers direct vs remote VT, borescope/videoscope, drones & ROVs, illumination > 1,000 lux, Jaeger J1 vision, ASME V Article 9, AWS D1.1 Clause 5.15, ISO 17637.

By Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III · May 16, 2026

Visual Testing (VT): The Complete 2026 Guide

Visual testing (VT) is the original, most-performed, and most-underrated non-destructive testing method. By the simplest possible means — the human eye, often augmented with mirrors, magnifiers, illumination, and increasingly with borescopes, videoscopes, drones and remote visual inspection (RVI) systems — VT detects surface conditions: cracks, corrosion, mechanical damage, weld profile, distortion, paint, coatings, foreign objects and dimensional irregularities. Every other NDT method is a follow-up to VT; ASME Section V Article 9 mandates VT as the prerequisite for any other examination. Modern VT extends from direct eye-on-part inspection at arm's length to high-definition videoscopy of jet-engine combustion chambers, deep-water ROV inspection of subsea wellheads, and AI-augmented drone-based bridge surveys. The method is governed by ASME V Article 9, ASTM E165 (cross-referenced), AWS D1.1 Clause 5.15 and 8.9, API 510/570/653 in-service codes, ISO 17637 (welds) and ISO 18238 (vision). This 2026 complete guide — written by ASNT Level III practitioners — covers physics, equipment, step-by-step procedure, codes, certifications, applications, common defects, advantages, costs and 2024-2026 innovations.

Physics & Principles of Visual Testing

VT relies on the physiology and physics of human vision augmented by optical instruments. Three vision parameters govern detection capability:

Visual acuity — the ability to resolve fine detail at a defined distance — is the primary qualifier. Code-compliant VT personnel are required to demonstrate near-vision acuity of Jaeger J1 (lines 0.4 mm at 300 mm) or equivalent (e.g. Snellen 20/25). Acuity is tested annually for code-compliant work per ASME V T-922 and ISO 9712 — eye exam, with corrective lenses if needed.

Color vision — verified via Ishihara plates or equivalent at hire and at least every 5 years — ensures the inspector can distinguish typical defect colors (oxide colors on heat-tinted stainless, paint colors, corrosion product colors).

Contrast sensitivity — the ability to detect a small luminance difference from background — depends on illumination level. ASME V T-952 mandates ≥ 1,000 lux at the inspection surface (some codes require 1,500 lux for fine work). Direct-VT illumination must be reasonably uniform without glare or shadow.

Beyond direct vision, three optical phenomena underpin equipment-aided VT:

Optical magnification via hand-held magnifiers (3-10×), loupes, or microscopes — extends practical resolution to ≤ 0.05 mm. Reflection via mirrors for hidden surfaces (e.g. inside-of-tube inspection during fabrication). Endoscopy via flexible (fiberscopes) or rigid (borescopes) tube assemblies, or video-equipped tip articulating videoscopes — extends visibility into pressure vessel interiors, pipework, gear cases, turbines and any cavity inaccessible to direct eye-on-part. Modern videoscope optics deliver > 1080p HD resolution at probe-tip distances of 5-150 mm, with stereo measurement (laser-shadow or stereo dual-lens) for sizing defects.

Remote Visual Inspection (RVI) extends VT to environments inhospitable to humans — pressure-vessel interiors during downtime, jet engines without disassembly, subsea oilfield infrastructure, nuclear reactor internals — using crawler robots, ROVs, drones and articulating snake-arm cameras.

Step-by-Step Visual Testing Procedure

  1. Pre-job planning & documentation review. Review the qualified VT procedure (per ASME V T-921 / ISO 17637). Confirm: scope of inspection, required acceptance criteria (AWS D1.1, ASME B31.3, API 510/570/653), reporting format, lighting requirement, surface preparation expectation. Verify the inspector's current annual eye exam is on file.
  2. Personnel preparation. Verify inspector has current ASNT Level II VT (or ISO 9712 / equivalent). Allow eyes to adapt to ambient conditions for at least 1 minute. If transitioning from bright sunlight to a dim vessel interior, allow 5-10 minutes dark-adaption.
  3. Surface preparation. Surface must be sufficiently clean to allow detection of relevant features. Per ASME V T-953 the surface is normally as-fabricated unless contractually specified otherwise. Remove loose scale, slag, weld spatter that could mask defects. For coated/painted in-service work, may require localized paint removal in any suspect area before measurement.
  4. Illumination & access setup. Verify illumination ≥ 1,000 lux at the inspection surface with a calibrated light meter. Some codes (e.g. ASME V T-952 for direct VT) accept 1,000 lux but 1,500 lux is preferred for fine fatigue cracks and corrosion pitting. Position direction of light to maximize defect visibility — generally low-angle grazing light reveals surface relief defects better than perpendicular flood-light. Ensure inspector can position eye within 600 mm of surface and at ≥ 30° angle for direct VT.
  5. Direct visual examination. Systematically scan the surface — top to bottom, left to right, in overlapping strips no more than 250 mm wide. Use 5×-10× loupe for fine inspection of weld toes, geometric transitions, suspected indications. Use a mirror to view hidden surfaces (inside of nozzles, back of fillets). Note every relevant feature: cracks, undercut, overlap, porosity, slag, spatter, arc strikes, mismatch (Hi-Lo), reinforcement profile, throat dimension, leg length.
  6. Measurement of relevant indications. Use weld gauge set for profile dimensions per AWS D1.1 Figure 5.5: reinforcement, undercut depth, fillet leg length and throat, Hi-Lo, concavity, convexity. Use pit gauge or depth micrometer for corrosion pits, mechanical damage. Use UT thickness gauge for wall-thinning if accessible.
  7. Remote visual examination (if applicable). For inaccessible surfaces (vessel interiors, piping bores, turbine internals), deploy borescope or videoscope: pre-clean the access port, articulate the probe to systematic positions (typically 360° rotation every 250 mm advance), record video of full coverage, freeze-frame for measurements via stereo or shadow technique. Verify probe-tip resolution against a reference scale before each shift.
  8. Indication marking & mapping. Mark all relevant indications with a paint marker. Photograph with a scale included. Sketch indication map showing weld ID, indication type, location and dimension. Record in inspection log.
  9. Accept / reject determination. Apply governing acceptance criteria. Common references: AWS D1.1 Table 8.1 (statically loaded), Table 8.2 (cyclically loaded), ASME B31.3 Section 341.3.2, API 510/570 in-service criteria. Cracks of any size — almost universally rejected.
  10. Reporting. Issue VT report listing procedure number, inspector certification level, area covered, lighting, equipment used, indications mapped, accept/reject decisions, Level II signature, Level III review for procedure qualification.

Standards & Codes Governing Visual Testing

ASME Boiler & Pressure Vessel Code Section V Article 9 — primary North American procedural standard. Defines direct visual examination (eye to surface < 600 mm at ≥ 30°), remote visual (lighting, resolution, recording), surface preparation, vision acuity (Jaeger J1 + colour Ishihara), illumination (≥ 1,000 lux at surface). Invoked by Section VIII (vessels), B31.1, B31.3, Section III nuclear, Section IX welding. Article 9 is paired with the in-service codes API 510, 570, 653.

ASME Section V Mandatory Appendix III covers Remote Visual Inspection (RVI) specifically, including borescope and videoscope resolution and recording requirements. Mandatory Appendix IV covers system performance verification.

AWS D1.1 Clause 5.15 defines the visual acceptance criteria for structural welds — the most-cited dimensional criteria in the world. Clause 8.9 covers fabrication-level VT. Tables 8.1 and 8.2 list specific accept/reject limits for cracks, undercut, fillet leg length, weld profile, etc.

ISO 17637 — Visual Testing of Fusion-Welded Joints. ISO 18238 covers vision requirements (acuity, illumination, colour). EN 13018 — VT general principles (largely superseded by ISO 17637 in 2016).

ASTM E165 cross-references VT as a prerequisite to PT. ASTM E1316 defines terminology. ASTM E3022 is the lighting standard (applies to UV but also informs VT lighting).

API 510 / 570 / 653 in-service inspection codes invoke VT as the principal in-service surface NDT method. NACE / AMPP SP 0294 / RP 0292 covers visual coating-condition inspection.

VT Inspector Certification Pathways

VT has the lowest formal-training threshold of any NDT method but the most onerous physical-eye-test requirement — annual vision verification mandatory.

ASNT SNT-TC-1A / CP-189: Level I VT requires 8 hours of training plus 70 hours of supervised OJT. Level II adds 16 hours (24 total) and 140 hours OJT. Level III requires the basic, method and specific exams plus 4 years documented experience. The vision exam is mandatory annually: Jaeger J1 or equivalent + Ishihara colour. Loss or expiration of vision certification immediately disqualifies. See the ASNT certification roadmap.

ISO 9712 / PCN / CSWIP: Level II VT requires 24 hours training + 1 month supervised experience (70 hours minimum), external exam, vision test, 5-year recertification.

AWS Certified Welding Inspector (CWI): The dominant U.S. weld VT certification — requires high-school education, 5 years of welding/inspection experience (or less with associate/bachelor degree), passing a 6-hour fundamentals + practical + code-book exam. Recertified every 9 years with annual vision exam. Many fabricators require CWI in addition to ASNT Level II VT. See our CWI certification guide.

For inspectors who specify and review VT — the pressure-vessel, piping and storage-tank inspector — the API certifications are the natural progression: API 510 Pressure Vessel, API 570 Piping, API 653 Storage Tank.

Applications by Industry

Oil & Gas: Pre-weld fit-up inspection, in-process root-bead VT, cap-pass VT, in-service vessel/piping VT during turnaround. ASME B31.3 mandates VT before any further NDT. API 510 / 570 / 653 use VT as the principal in-service surface method.

Power Generation: Steam-turbine blade VT during overhaul (borescope), boiler tube external VT, HRSG internals VT via crawler.

Aerospace: Engine borescope inspection between flights and at overhaul intervals — combustion chamber, turbine blades, compressor airfoils. Airframe surface VT during heavy maintenance (C/D-check) finds skin fatigue cracks, corrosion, lightning-strike damage. See our aircraft engine component inspection.

Nuclear: Reactor pressure-vessel internals VT via underwater RVI cameras, RPV closure-head bolt VT, control-rod-drive VT. Some primary system inspections require < 0.4 mm resolution at probe-tip working distance per Mandatory Appendix IV.

Manufacturing: Production-line VT of castings, forgings, machined parts — increasingly automated with machine vision.

Marine & Shipbuilding: Hull external VT (dry-dock, ROV-based wet inspection), tank internal VT, anchor-chain VT.

Bridge & Civil Infrastructure: Drone-based VT of bridges, towers, wind-turbine blades. See our bridge inspection guide and wind turbine blade inspection.

Advantages & Limitations of Visual Testing

Advantages: Fastest of any NDT method — 1-5 minutes per joint. Cheapest — $0.05-$0.20 per joint consumables. No surface chemistry, electrical power or radiation hazard. Universally applicable to any material — steel, aluminum, plastic, composite, ceramic. Detects surface conditions invisible to other NDT methods — coatings, profile, geometric mismatch. Mandatory prerequisite to any other NDT (ASME V T-921). RVI extends reach to internal cavities. Easy to document with photo evidence. Inspectors can be qualified relatively quickly (8-24 hours classroom).

Limitations: Only detects surface and externally-visible defects (no subsurface capability). Sensitive to operator vision and fatigue; long inspection days produce errors. Cracks < 25 μm wide are typically invisible to unaided eye (require magnification). Borescope and videoscope have limited depth of field. RVI in confined spaces requires permit-to-work and gas-test entry. Color-tint detection on stainless requires good lighting and may require specific lamp temperature (3,000-4,000 K). Critically dependent on lighting quality and surface cleanliness. Highly subjective without rigorous procedure and calibrated tools.

Cost & ROI of Visual Testing

Field VT is the cheapest NDT inspection by labor and consumables. Typical 2026 rates: butt-weld VT on structural steel, $5-$12 per joint. Pressure-vessel internal VT during turnaround, $1,200-$3,500 per vessel (3-8 hours). Borescope inspection of a 100-cm-long heat-exchanger tube, $25-$50 per tube. Direct VT Procedure Qualification & Inspector Vision Records

Visual testing's deceptive simplicity masks rigorous qualification requirements. Every code-compliant VT procedure must be qualified — typically by Level III approval and demonstration on a representative test piece showing that the smallest specified defect is detected under the procedure's lighting and access conditions.

Essential variables per ASME V T-921: surface preparation, lighting type and intensity, access geometry (direct vs remote), required equipment (mirrors, magnifiers, gauges), inspector vision requirements, recording and acceptance criteria. Any change in an essential variable requires re-qualification.

The inspector vision record is the single most important personnel document. Per ASME V T-922 and ISO 9712, every VT inspector must demonstrate annually: (1) near-vision Jaeger J1 (or equivalent Snellen 20/25) on a standard near-vision chart at 300 mm with corrective lenses if needed, (2) colour-vision Ishihara plates at hire and at least every 5 years. The record is maintained by the certifying authority (the company Level III for ASNT, the central body for ISO 9712). Loss of vision certification immediately suspends the inspector from code work — no exceptions.

For high-stakes nuclear and aerospace work, the requirement is often stricter: ASME Section XI (in-service inspection of nuclear power plants) requires Jaeger J2 (lines 0.6 mm at 300 mm — slightly easier than J1) per IWA-2321 with annual re-test, plus a demonstration of resolution at the actual working distance using a custom resolution target.

Remote Visual Inspection: Borescope, Videoscope & ROV Technical Detail

RVI is the fastest-evolving area of VT. Three main equipment classes.

Rigid borescopes use a series of relay lenses inside a stainless steel tube. Diameter 4-10 mm; working length 175-500 mm typical (extreme cases to 2 m for industrial applications). Optical resolution < 0.05 mm at the tip working distance of 25-50 mm. Pen-style economy models use a simple eyepiece; professional models couple to a video camera. Used for: cylinder bore inspection, blind-tapped hole inspection, gun barrel inspection, jet engine intermediate inspection.

Flexible fiberscopes use a coherent bundle of optical fibers (typically 6,000-30,000 fibers, each < 10 μm diameter) to transmit the image through a bendable shaft. Diameter 4-12 mm; working length 1-3 m. Resolution limited by fiber count (typically 0.5 mm at tip), so quickly being replaced by videoscopes. Still used where electromagnetic interference precludes electronic videoscope use.

Videoscopes place a CMOS / CCD sensor and LED light source at the probe tip, transmitting digital video back through a flexible shaft. Diameter 6-12 mm typical; working length 1-3 m. 4-way articulation at the tip. HD or 4K resolution. Stereo measurement via two cameras at the tip, or shadow measurement via offset LED — both give 0.1 mm dimensional accuracy at 25 mm tip-to-target distance. The market leaders: Olympus IPLEX NX, GE Mentor Visual iQ, Karl Storz, Yateks. Capital cost $25,000-$75,000 for handheld; $150,000-$400,000 for advanced articulated systems with 3D mapping.

Inspection ROVs and crawlers extend RVI to environments where a handheld probe cannot reach — submerged subsea infrastructure (SaaB Seaeye, VideoRay), large vessel interiors (GE Inuktun crawlers, snake-arm devices). HD camera plus auxiliary lighting plus often UT thickness gauging in a single platform. ROVs deploy from a surface vessel or platform to depths of 1,000-3,000 m for offshore inspection. See our offshore platform inspection guide.

Drone-Based Inspection: Regulations, Capability & Workflow

Drone-based VT has matured rapidly. The dominant 2026 platforms: DJI Matrice 30T (commercial workhorse, RTK GPS, IR + 4K camera), Skydio X2 (semi-autonomous obstacle avoidance), FlyAbility Elios 3 (collision-tolerant indoor / confined-space inspection with lidar SLAM).

The standard external-asset drone-VT workflow: pre-job site survey, flight-permission filing (FAA Part 107 in U.S., CASR Part 101 in Australia, EASA Part-UAS in EU); pre-flight: charge batteries, calibrate compass, verify return-to-home setpoint, set geofence; flight: fly a planned grid pattern at 5-15 m standoff capturing overlapping 80 % nadir + 20 % oblique images; post-flight: stitch images via photogrammetry software (Pix4D, Agisoft Metashape) into a dimensioned 3D model; review: a Level II VT inspector reviews the imagery in-office, flags candidate indications, dispatches a follow-up ground team to suspect areas. The drone replaces 60-80 % of scaffolding and rope-access labor.

For confined-space indoor inspection (storage tank interiors, boiler interiors, ship cargo holds), the collision-tolerant Elios 3 carries a 4K camera plus a lidar SLAM module that builds a real-time interior 3D map. Indoor flights bypass the permit-to-work requirements for human entry — a typical 30-meter-diameter tank that previously required 8 hours of confined-space-entry inspection can be drone-scanned in 30 minutes. ROI: typically > 90 % labor savings on first-year program.

VT Standards Comparison Across Codes & Acceptance Tables

The single biggest source of VT field error is using one code's acceptance criteria when a different code applies. The dominant 2026 visual acceptance tables:

AWS D1.1 Table 8.1 (statically loaded non-tubular connections): explicit limits for crack (none permitted), undercut depth (0.25 mm for thicker material), porosity (cluster < 6 mm), fillet leg dimension (per design + 1.5 mm tolerance). Most-cited table for structural welding worldwide.

AWS D1.1 Table 8.2 (cyclically loaded): tighter limits for fatigue applications — undercut allowed only at toes parallel to the principal stress, etc.

ASME B31.3 Section 341.3.2 Normal Fluid Service: visual criteria refer to BPVC Section IX qualification plus specific dimensional limits on weld profile.

ASME B31.3 Section 341.3.2 Severe Cyclic / Category M: tighter limits including no crack, no LOF, no overlap, undercut depth restrictions.

API 510 Section 5.5 (in-service vessel VT): focus on corrosion features, mechanical damage, distortion, leakage — different paradigm from new-construction VT.

API 570 Section 5.5 (in-service piping VT): similar in-service focus.

API 653 Section 6 (storage tank VT): roof, shell and floor visual inspection with sketch and photo documentation.

Always confirm which code applies before quoting acceptance.

VT Case Study: 30-Year Refinery Pressure Vessel Re-Rating

A 30-year-old refinery surge drum (1995-vintage, 4.5 m ID × 12 m long, ASME Section VIII Div 1) underwent a 2026 fitness-for-service re-rating using a drone-plus-RVI internal VT campaign. External drone inspection (DJI M30T) captured 4K imagery of all 600 m² of vessel shell and head exterior in 90 minutes, with photogrammetric reconstruction into a 3D digital twin. Internal inspection used an Elios 3 confined-space drone (no human entry) followed by handheld Olympus IPLEX NX videoscope inspection of 24 nozzle bore welds and 6 internal-baffle attachment welds. Total indications identified: 3 hairline cracks at saddle support welds (later confirmed by MT), 14 corrosion-pit clusters (mapped and UT-thickness-verified), localized blistering at one HAZ. The vessel was re-rated for 5 more years of service at ≈ $35,000 inspection cost vs an alternative full-scaffold internal-entry inspection at $280,000 plus 5 additional turnaround days. The captured 3D model is loaded to the Atlantis Digital Twins platform for ongoing integrity-trend monitoring. This is a typical 2026 ROI of drone + RVI VT on a major pressure-equipment asset.

Procurement, Service Sourcing & Buyer Checklist for VT

VT is the most-commoditized NDT method, which makes vendor differentiation harder for buyers — and the cost of a poor VT inspector higher because every other NDT method depends on first-line VT accuracy. The five-item buyer checklist:

(1) Personnel certification. ASNT Level II VT (or ISO 9712 Level II) for every inspector, with current annual vision exam (Jaeger J1 / Snellen 20/25 + Ishihara). For weld inspection in fabrication, an additional AWS Certified Welding Inspector (CWI) certificate is broadly expected — see our CWI certification guide. For in-service pressure equipment inspection, supervising inspector should hold API 510, API 570 or API 653 as applicable.

(2) Equipment kit. Verify the field kit contains calibrated weld gauge set, pit gauge, calibrated lux meter, mirror set, magnifier (at least 5×), pen-style borescope, DSLR or equivalent camera with macro lens. For RVI work, additionally a code-compliant videoscope (resolution demonstrable to Mandatory Appendix III requirements) and a probe-tip resolution reference target.

(3) Written procedure. VT procedure listing the essential variables (surface preparation, lighting, vision, equipment, acceptance) signed by Level III. For each project, a project-specific Annex documenting acceptance code reference (e.g. AWS D1.1 Table 8.1, ASME B31.3 Section 341.3.2, API 510).

(4) Lighting and access plan. For new-construction work: confirm shop lighting at the inspection location ≥ 1,000 lux. For field/in-service work: portable LED inspection lights and a lux meter — verify illumination at each weld before inspection.

(5) Reporting format. Verify the deliverable format: hand-sketched indication maps are obsolete; modern code-compliant reporting uses mobile photo-tagged indication records with weld ID, GPS coordinates, dimensional measurements and accept/reject disposition. The Atlantis NDT reporting platform is purpose-built for this workflow.

Typical 2026 VT crew day rates: $650-$1,100 U.S., $450-$850 Middle East, $250-$550 India / SE Asia. CWI-supervised structural weld VT: $5-$12 per joint. Pressure-vessel internal VT during turnaround: $1,200-$3,500 per vessel. Drone-based external VT of a refinery tower: $5,000-$15,000 per day with photogrammetric 3D model deliverable. Subsea ROV VT: $25,000-$75,000 per day-rate. For asset owners, ROI of investing in higher-quality VT (better-certified inspectors, more rigorous lighting/access, mobile digital reporting) typically pays back in the first turnaround through avoided rework, faster downstream NDT scheduling, and improved fitness-for-service documentation for ASME and API code compliance.

Frequently Asked Questions about Visual Testing

Q1: What lighting level is required for code-compliant VT?

A: Minimum 1,000 lux at the inspection surface per ASME V T-952. 1,500-2,000 lux preferred for fine work (fatigue cracks, corrosion pitting). Measure with a calibrated lux meter held at the surface.

Q2: What is direct vs remote visual examination?

A: Direct = eye to surface < 600 mm at angle ≥ 30°. Remote = via borescope, videoscope, mirror, camera or any other optical aid. ASME V Article 9 covers both; Mandatory Appendix III specifically governs RVI resolution and recording.

Q3: What vision requirements must VT personnel meet?

A: Annual near-vision acuity Jaeger J1 (lines 0.4 mm at 300 mm) or equivalent Snellen 20/25 — with corrective lenses if needed. Colour-vision Ishihara plates at hire and at least every 5 years. Failure of either disqualifies the inspector from code work until re-tested and passed.

Q4: How do I qualify a VT procedure to ASME V?

A: Write procedure per T-921 covering scope, lighting, surface condition, equipment, vision aids, acceptance criteria. Demonstrate on representative test piece showing required indication is visible. Level III approval mandatory.

Q5: What is the minimum probe-tip resolution for borescope inspection?

A: Per ASME V Mandatory Appendix III, probe-tip resolution must be demonstrated against a 1 mm or 0.4 mm reference at the working distance specified in the procedure. Modern HD videoscopes easily achieve < 0.1 mm at 25 mm WD.

Q6: Can drones be used for code-compliant VT?

A: Yes — provided the resolution, lighting, recording and Level II review meet ASME V Article 9 and Mandatory Appendix III. Drones are increasingly used for bridges, tanks, towers and flare stacks where access is hazardous.

Q7: What is the relationship between VT and other NDT methods?

A: VT is the mandatory prerequisite to any other NDT method per ASME V T-921 (and any owner-specified procedure). Any surface treatment defect (slag, scale, paint over-coverage) that would interfere with PT/MT/UT/RT must be addressed before those methods are applied.

Q8: What weld profile gauges should I carry?

A: Cambridge gauge (universal — covers convexity, concavity, fillet leg, throat, undercut depth). Hi-Lo gauge (root mismatch and reinforcement). Bridge cam (fillet leg). Fillet weld gauge set (multiple leg dimensions). Pit gauge / depth micrometer for corrosion.

Q9: When is direct VT inadequate and RVI required?

A: Any time the inspector cannot achieve eye-to-surface distance < 600 mm at angle ≥ 30°. Pressure-vessel interiors, piping bores, turbine internals, heat-exchanger tubes, gear-case interiors are all RVI applications.

Q10: What is heat tint on stainless steel and why does it matter?

A: Surface oxide color formed during welding — light straw (260 °C) to dark blue (430 °C). Heat tint indicates chromium oxide depletion and locally reduced corrosion resistance. ASME B31.3 normal-fluid service requires removal by pickling/passivation for stainless service.

Q11: Can a CWI certification substitute for ASNT VT Level II?

A: Per ASME V T-921, only an ASNT Level II VT (or equivalent ISO 9712 / NAS 410) is recognized for code VT. AWS CWI is widely accepted for welding-visual inspection by fabrication standards but ASME-stamped work requires ASNT or equivalent Level II VT in addition.

Q12: How do I record evidence of a VT finding?

A: Photograph with a measurement scale included. For RVI, freeze-frame video and save in a tamper-evident archive (DICONDE compliant for nuclear/aerospace). Use Atlantis NDT's mobile reporting platform to tag photos to weld ID, GPS location, timestamp, inspector ID and procedure revision.

Q13: What is the difference between AWS visual acceptance and ASME visual acceptance?

A: AWS D1.1 (structural) has explicit dimensional acceptance tables (Tables 8.1 statically and 8.2 cyclically loaded). ASME B31.3 (process piping) references ASME V Article 9 and Section IX without specific dimensional tables — relies on procedure-specified acceptance. Both reject any crack.

Q14: Can I do VT on hot surfaces?

A: Up to about 150 °C with normal PPE; above that, use heat-resistant mirrors or remote camera. RVI is the standard for hot equipment (still-warm vessels, in-operation pipework).

Q15: How does VT interface with API 510 / 570 / 653 in-service inspection?

A: Each of these in-service codes mandates VT as the primary external survey of the vessel/piping/tank, with UT thickness used for wall-loss measurement and PT/MT for crack-confirmation. The API inspector schedules and approves VT, but the work itself is typically performed by an ASNT Level II VT under the API inspector's direction.
